questions.q: Why does this lesson describe dashboards, logs, and drift reports as 'pull-based' and alerting as 'push-based'?
options: A dashboard requires someone to open it and look, while an alert notices a threshold crossing and notifies a person automatically
Pull-based and push-based mean exactly the same thing in this lesson
Dashboards automatically notify every user the moment any data changes
Alerts require a person to manually check them every hour
questions.explain: Dashboards wait for someone to go look; alerting flips that by having the system notify a person when a threshold is crossed.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three things does a working alert definition actually need?
options: A favorite color, a random number, and a user's email signature
A metric to watch, a numeric threshold, and the time window that threshold is measured over
Only a metric — thresholds and time windows are optional
A screenshot of the dashboard and nothing else
questions.explain: An alert needs a specific metric, a threshold that distinguishes normal variance from a real problem, and the window that threshold applies over.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a triggered alert needs to be routed somewhere a human will actually see it, like Slack or email?
options: A rule that fires into a void is no better than having no rule at all — the information needs to reach a person who can act on it
Routing alerts to a human is purely decorative and has no practical benefit
Alerts that aren't routed anywhere automatically fix the underlying problem
Email and Slack are the only channels alerts can ever be sent to
questions.explain: An alert that triggers but reaches no one accomplishes nothing — it needs to land where a person will see it and can act.

questions.q: What is 'alert fatigue,' as this lesson describes it?
options: A technical error that prevents any alerts from ever firing
When every minor fluctuation triggers a notification, the team stops reading them, and the one alert that actually matters gets lost in the noise
A feature that automatically silences all alerts permanently
The amount of money an alerting system costs per month
questions.explain: Over-alerting on everything causes a team to tune out notifications entirely, defeating the purpose of having alerts at all.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a system with perfect logging, drift detection, and hallucination scoring could still fail its users badly without alerting?
options: Because logging and scoring automatically prevent all failures regardless of alerting
Because none of those signals matter unless something routes the information to a person who can act on it in time
Because alerting makes logging and drift detection entirely unnecessary
Because hallucination scoring requires alerting to function at all
questions.explain: Every monitoring signal built up in this chapter is pull-based — without alerting pushing the information to someone, a real problem can go unnoticed for far too long.
